overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Mechanics of Redemption
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 11a–11b
overview.hebrewSource: עַיִן יָפָה בְּסֶלַע, עַיִן רָעָה בְּשֶׁקֶל, בֵּינוֹנִית בְּרִגְיָא
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf works through the practical mechanics of redeeming a firstborn donkey: how little the redeeming lamb may be worth, and what to do when one has no lamb at all. Reish Lakish permits redeeming with cash equal to the donkey's value, prompting a search for whose opinion this follows and why it holds even for the stricter view. The Gemara then asks whether redeeming a neighbor's donkey without being asked is even valid, works through a multi-generation inheritance case involving priests and Israelites, and closes by pinpointing the exact moment a designated lamb legally becomes the priest's.

slides.title: 💰 How Much Must the Redeeming Lamb Be Worth?
slides.subtitle: The letter of the law, sage guidance, and practical halakha
rows: Rav Yosef / Rava (letter of the law)
Any value works — even a lean lamb worth a single ma'ah (a small fraction of a shekel)
Generous: a sela (4 dinars); miserly: a shekel (2 dinars); average: a ragya (3 dinars)
One who comes to ask a sage is told to give a ragya — but one who redeems on his own with less has still fulfilled the mitzva

callout.label: No real contradiction:
callout.text: The strict letter of the law permits any value; someone who consults a sage first is simply held to the recommended middle standard.

slides.title: 🥬 Redeeming With Money Instead of a Lamb
slides.subtitle: What if you have a firstborn donkey but no lamb?

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: One who has a firstborn donkey but no lamb may redeem it with money equal to its value.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: Whose view is this? Not Rabbi Yehuda — he insists the Torah is particular that redemption be specifically with a lamb! It must be Rabbi Shimon.

lines.speaker: Ravina
lines.text: But the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and an unattributed mishna already follows him too — so how can Reish Lakish rule like Rabbi Shimon?

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Even Rabbi Yehuda agrees: a firstborn donkey shouldn't be more stringent than ordinary consecrated property, redeemable with any valuables. 'With a lamb' was stated to be lenient — a lamb costs less than the donkey — not to restrict the medium.

callout.label: In practice:
callout.text: Rav Naḥman, son of Rav Yosef, redeemed a firstborn donkey with boiled vegetables worth its full value.

slides.title: 🐴 Redeeming Someone Else's Firstborn Donkey
slides.subtitle: Is it valid, and who owns the donkey afterward?

nodes.content: ❓ If I redeem my neighbor's firstborn donkey without being asked, is the redemption valid? And whose donkey is it afterward?
✅ Rav Huna: the redemption is valid — but a dilemma remains about ownership afterward

columns.label: According to R' Shimon
columns.content: No dilemma — since benefit was already permitted beforehand, the donkey was always the original owner's property

columns.label: According to R' Yehuda
columns.content: Real dilemma — like redeeming consecrated property (redeemer acquires it), or does the owner keep rights since a lamb costs less than full value?

nodes.content: ✅ Resolved from theft law: a thief who steals it pays the ORIGINAL OWNER double — proving he retains rights, unlike ownerless consecrated property (no double payment for stealing from the Temple)

slides.title: 👪 Three Generations, Ten Donkeys
slides.subtitle: Inherited uncertainty across a priest-Israelite lineage

steps.content: 1️⃣ An Israelite has ten donkeys of uncertain firstborn status. He designates ten lambs and keeps them all — the priest can't prove any specific one is owed
2️⃣ Trickier case: ten certainly firstborn donkeys, inherited from a priest grandfather — who himself inherited them, still unredeemed, from HIS Israelite grandfather
3️⃣ Ruling: the Israelite grandson designates ten lambs and keeps them all — treated as if his priest grandfather had already separated and acquired the lambs himself
4️⃣ A parallel ruling applies to inherited untithed produce passed the same priest-then-Israelite route — both cases had to be stated separately, since each could otherwise be explained away

slides.title: ☠️ When Does the Priest Acquire the Redeeming Lamb?
slides.subtitle: Pinpointing the exact legal moment

nodes.content: ❓ The mishna: 'if the lamb dies, one may derive benefit from it.' At what point does the lamb become the priest's?
🤔 Obvious cases dismissed: if it died already in the priest's house, of course he may benefit from his own property
✅ Real novelty: from the very moment of designation by the owner — even before it physically reaches the priest's hand — the lamb is already legally his

summary.principle: A firstborn donkey may be redeemed with a lamb of nearly any value — or with equivalent money if none is available — and once a lamb is designated for redemption, it belongs to the priest from that instant, whether or not it has physically changed hands.

flowSteps.content: 💰 Redemption requires only minimal value by strict law, though sage guidance recommends a ragya (3 dinars)
🥬 Without a lamb, money of equal value suffices — reconciled even with Rabbi Yehuda's stricter view

columns.content: 🐴 A neighbor's donkey may be redeemed by another; theft law proves the original owner retains rights beforehand
👪 Inherited uncertain or unredeemed firstborns pass with their lambs intact across generations

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a designated redeeming lamb belongs to the priest from the moment of designation, not from physical delivery

quiz.q: According to Rava's practical ruling, what must one give when consulting a sage about redeeming a firstborn donkey — and does a lesser amount work if done independently?
o: A full sela is required in all cases
A ragya (about 3 dinars) is recommended when asking a sage, but redeeming independently with even a lean lamb worth one ma'ah fulfills the obligation
Only money may be used, never a lamb
The lamb must be unblemished and full-grown
quiz.e: Rava rules that one who consults a sage is directed to a ragya, but the letter of the law permits redemption with a lamb of any value, even a single ma'ah, if done independently.

quiz.q: How does Ravina reconcile Reish Lakish's ruling (that money may redeem a firstborn donkey) with Rabbi Yehuda's position that the Torah insists on a lamb?
o: He says Reish Lakish must be wrong
A firstborn donkey should not be more stringent than consecrated property; 'with a lamb' was stated to be lenient (cheaper), not to restrict the redemption medium
He says Rabbi Yehuda only applies to donkeys, not money
He claims the two never actually disagree
quiz.e: Ravina explains that the requirement of a lamb makes redemption easier (since a lamb is worth less than the donkey), not harder — so money of equal value should also work even according to Rabbi Yehuda.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara prove that the original owner retains rights to an unredeemed firstborn donkey, rather than it being ownerless like consecrated property?
o: From a direct verse stating so
From the law of theft — a thief who steals it must pay the owner double payment, which would not apply to theft from the Temple treasury
From the fact that donkeys cannot be consecrated
From Rabbi Shimon's opinion alone
quiz.e: The double payment owed to the owner for theft proves ownership remains with him even before redemption, unlike stealing from consecrated Temple property, which incurs no such double payment.

quiz.q: In the case of an Israelite who inherits ten certainly-firstborn donkeys from a priest grandfather (who himself inherited them, unredeemed, from an Israelite grandfather), what may the grandson do?
o: Nothing — the donkeys must be given entirely to a priest
He designates ten lambs, tithes them, and keeps them all, as if his priest grandfather had already acquired the lambs
He must sell the donkeys to a gentile
He may only keep five of the ten lambs
quiz.e: The ruling treats the situation as though the priest grandfather had already separated and acquired the redeeming lambs, so his Israelite grandson inherits full rights to all ten.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's resolution of the mishna's statement that one may benefit from a dead redemption lamb, from what moment does the lamb belong to the priest?
o: Only once it physically reaches the priest's hand
From the moment the owner designates it, even before it reaches the priest
Only after the priest formally accepts it in front of witnesses
The lamb never truly belongs to the priest
quiz.e: The novelty taught is that designation alone transfers the lamb into the priest's possession, so even if it dies beforehand while still with the owner, the priest may derive benefit from it.
